newsitem.title: USA: Republican chief says party must broaden appeal.
newsitem.headline: Republican chief says party must broaden appeal.

text.p: Retiring Republican Party chairman Haley Barbour said Thursday his party must reach out to women and minorities or risk facing a Democratic comeback.

In a farewell address to the Republican National Committee, Barbour, who is stepping down after four years as chairman, urged colleagues not to be satisfied with merely controlling Congress. To truly implement its visions, it needed to win the White House in 2000.

"Without the presidency our policies are easily sidetracked or watered down ... We are the national majority but we must elect a Republican president for that national majority to truly govern," he said.
Barbour said the party failed in the 1996 presidential election because it did not communicate effectively with women, Hispanics and blacks.
The 165-member committee will elect Barbour's successor Friday with eight candidates vying for the post.

"We are failing today to effectively communicate to many women and minorities why our proposals are the right policies to solve the problems that concern them most, and our failure to connect creates an opening for the Democrats," he said.
Among male voters President Clinton lost to Republican Bob Dole by one percentage point in last November's presidential election. Among women, Clinton outpolled Dole by 16 points.

Barbour, who helped guide Republicans to a 1994 electoral triumph when the party took control of both houses of Congress for the first time in 40 years, argued that many women agreed in principle with Republican ideas on lower taxes, reforming welfare and giving greater school choice.
But, he said, the party never explained to those voters the reasons behind those policies and how they would affect the quality of life for all Americans.
He said he sensed black voters were becoming disillusioned with the Democrats. "We must make it clear to them and other minorities that ... we welcome them with open arms," he said.

Barbour said Republicans should move with steady determination to dismantle what is left of the welfare state, while recognising that it would not be possible to do this in a single session of Congress.
